text: A. fumigatus is a species of fungus that can be found throughout the environment, including in household dust . Aspergillosis is the name of infections caused by Aspergillus species of fungi. One of the common forms of aspergillosis is an allergic reaction that occurs within the lungs and is seen in asthma patients , . Given this connection, an EoE model utilizing A. fumigatus was developed. Initially, Mishra and colleagues explored the connection between EoE and eosinophilic allergic responses within the lungs. Mice were administered A. fumigatus intranasally or intragastrically 3 times a week across 3 weeks with euthanasia occurring 18–20 hours after the final challenge . Intranasal treatment with A. fumigatus led to more robust esophageal eosinophilia within the lamina propria compared to oral gavage indicating that EoE occurs as a result of airway sensitization . Expanding on this protocol, Mishra et al., also challenged mice with A. fumigatus intratracheally, and found that both intranasal and intratracheal aeroallergen exposure promoted simultaneous esophageal and pulmonary eosinophilia. Immunohistochemical staining of A. fumigatus -treated esophageal tissue sections revealed significant increase of B cells, as well as CD4 + and CD8 + T cells . Furthermore, evidence of diminished esophageal eosinophil counts were observed in T cell-deficient mice but not B cell-deficient mice with A. fumigatus -driven EoE, indicating that CD4 + and CD8 + immune cell populations are critical for the recruitment of eosinophils , . The proinflammatory TRAIL pathway has been implicated in EoE pathogenesis through the use of egg antigen- and aeroallergen-drivendriven models in vivo . Esophagi of A. fumigatus -treated TRAIL-deficient ( Trail −/− ) mice exhibited diminished eosinophil and mast cell counts, inflammatory chemokine expression ( Ccl11, Ccl24 ), and remodeling compared to their TRAIL-proficient counterparts.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Esophagi of A. fumigatus -treated TRAIL-deficient ( Trail −/− ) mice exhibited diminished eosinophil and mast cell counts, inflammatory chemokine expression ( Ccl11, Ccl24 ), and remodeling compared to their TRAIL-proficient counterparts. The TRAIL pathway has also been reported to regulate Il-33 expression in vivo during liver injury . Interestingly, 24 hours of A. fumigatus treatment led to a five-fold increase in Il33 expression; however, Il33 levels returned to baseline by the completion of the first week of dosing and stayed comparable to control levels despite the occurrence of EoE pathologic features . Upregulation of microRNA, miR-223, expression was found to be associated with TRAIL in mice with A. fumigatus -driven EoE . Furthermore, miR-223 was revealed as a regulator of eosinophilia, epithelial remodeling, and Th2 cytokine expression in mice with EoE-like inflammation . A. fumigatus -treated IL-18-deficient mice or IL-18 neutralized mice were protected against EoE induction, demonstrating the critical role of IL-18 and the NLRP3/Caspase-1/IL-18 immune pathway in EoE pathogenesis . Notably, Niranjan and colleagues reported that A. fumigatus -driven esophageal eosinophilia and mast cell infiltration occurs independent of the IL-13/IL-4/STAT6 signaling axis . A. fumigatus has also been utilized to study host-microbiota interactions in EoE. In a study by Brusilovsky and colleagues, EoE was induced via sensitization with A. fumigatus and alum adjuvant via i.p. injection followed by challenge with intra-esophageal A. fumigatus for 2 consecutive days at 2-day intervals over a period of 3 weeks . Using this protocol, the investigators found that the esophageal microbiota of EoE mice undergoes a shift in which the Lactobacillales, which is dominant under homeostatic conditions, exhibit reduced abundance following induction of allergic inflammation.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Using this protocol, the investigators found that the esophageal microbiota of EoE mice undergoes a shift in which the Lactobacillales, which is dominant under homeostatic conditions, exhibit reduced abundance following induction of allergic inflammation. Given the ability of broad-spectrum antibiotics to induce dysbiosis and significantly affect Lactobacillales, investigators sought to determine if treatment with antibiotics at the preweaning stage would exacerbate type 2-associated esophageal inflammation later in life. A. fumigatus -treated mice that received antibiotics pre-weaning had higher esophageal eosinophil counts, as well as increased serum levels of allergen-specific IgE and decreased levels of allergen-specific IgG compared to control EoE mice. These mice also displayed increased serum levels of Th2 cytokines IL-13 and IL-5, while EoE mice that did not receive antibiotic treatment exhibited increased levels of Th1 cytokines, suggesting antibiotic use in early life and depletion of Lactobacillales promotes type 2 inflammation in the esophagus in response to environmental allergens . Holvoet and colleagues used A. fumigatus to investigate the influence of the probiotic Lactococcus lactis ( L. lactis ) on EoE pathogenesis. Mice were treated with A. fumigatus protein extract on a gauze patch applied to the skin followed by a 2-week rest period then another patch treatment from days 28 to 35 and finally an intranasal A. fumigatus challenge and euthanasia on day 38. When given as a therapeutic treatment to mice with A. fumigatus -mediated EoE, L. lactis NCC 2287 oral supplementation significantly reduced esophageal eosinophilic infiltration, suggesting that probiotics attenuate EoE-associated inflammation .
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Avlas and colleagues demonstrated the ability of 4-ethoxymethylene-2-phenyl-2-oxazolin (Oxazolone; OXA) to induce an EoE phenotype in mice with the overarching goal of understanding how IL-4 and IL-13 contribute to EoE via the type II IL-4 receptor . OXA is a known haptenizing agent, highlighting the rationale for utilizing this chemical in a murine model of EoE. To induce EoE, mice were epicutaneously sensitized on both ear flanks with OXA dissolved in acetone followed by six topical OXA challenges. After 18 days, mice were intra-esophageally challenged and then euthanized on day 36. OXA-treated mice produced a robust EoE phenotype, featuring esophageal eosinophilic infiltrates, thickening of the lamina propria and epithelium, and increased collagen deposition as compared to controls. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a 25% overlap between the genetic signature of mice with OXA-induced EoE and human subjects with EoE, with notable upregulation of Th2 cytokines and their receptors ( Il13 , Il13rα1 , and Il4rα ) as well eosinophil‐associated chemokines ( Ccl11 ). Furthermore, OXA-induced EoE was linked to epithelial production of IL-13 as either squamous epithelial-targeted IL-13Rα1 knockout ( Il13ra1 −/− , Krt14Cre;Il13ra1 fl/fl ) or antibody-based IL-13 neutralization inhibited EoE-like inflammation and tissue remodeling.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Recently, Doyle and colleagues established an allergen-driven EoE murine model utilizing sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) detergent, an environmental allergen found in common household products such as laundry detergent, toothpaste and cleaning supplies , . Given that SDS increases paracellular flux in normal human epidermal keratinocytes by downregulating Occludin and Claudin-1 , and that esophageal epithelial barrier defects are a hallmark of EoE – , , Doyle and colleagues sought to elucidate whether exposure to SDS detergent promoted EoE-specific esophageal epithelial dysfunction and inflammation. For these studies, mice were exposed to SDS in drinking water for 14 days . SDS treatment led to esophageal eosinophilia and BCH, along with increased Il33 expression, CD4 + T cell infiltration, and esophageal inflammation .

text: To generate these mice, the investigators generated two separate transgenic lines. The first carried the IL-13 gene under the control of TetO promoter while the second expressed the rtTA under the control of the Clara cell 10kD protein ( Cc10) promoter, which directs expression specifically in the lung epithelium. To induce EoE, Cc10-rtTA;TetO-il13 mice were fed DOX over the course of 30 days. In addition to increased IL-13 protein expression in the esophageal epithelium following DOX ingestion, esophagi of these mice featured transmural eosinophilia, epithelial remodeling, and increased vasculature , . This study further demonstrated that EoE-associated inflammation and tissue remodeling is eotaxin-1-mediated and occurs independent of eosinophil recruitment . Interestingly, vitamin D has been identified as a natural IL-13 antagonist . Investigators found that vitamin D levels were inversely related to severity of esophageal eosinophilia and epithelial histopathology in Cc10-rtTA;TetO-Il13 mice treated with DOX for 2 weeks . Mavi and colleagues utilized Cc10-rtTA;TetO-II13 mice to overexpress IL-13 with the goal of understanding the effect of prolonged EoE inflammation, more specifically eosinophils, on esophageal function by extending the feeding time of DOX from 30 days to 8 weeks . In addition to chronic eosinophilic and mast cell esophageal inflammation, investigators also assessed esophageal stricture via X-ray barium swallowing and found esophageal stricture had occurred following 8 weeks. Interestingly, following an 8-week period with no DOX-infused food, these strictures were still present despite the lack of esophageal eosinophilia, suggesting that IL-13 transgene-induced stricture may be an irreversible process and thus provides insight into EoE development and progression as well as a potential therapeutic target . CC10-rtTA;TetO-II13 mice have also been modified to study EoE pathobiology.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: CC10-rtTA;TetO-II13 mice have also been modified to study EoE pathobiology. For example, after observing increased expression of Resistin-like molecule ( Relm )- α in the esophageal epithelium of mice with allergen-induced EoE, Mavi et al. developed a Relm-α gene-inducible bitransgenic mouse ( Cc10-rtTA-Relmα ) to determine the functional role of Relm-α in EoE in vivo . In addition to significantly increased Relm-α protein expression, DOX-treated Cc10-rtTA-Relmα mice exhibited BCH and an accumulation of activated CD4 + and CD4 − T cell subsets . Esophageal eosinophilia occurred in DOX-treated Cc10-rtTA-Relmα mice, with no change in the expression of eosinophil active cytokines IL-5, IL-13, eotaxin-1, or eotaxin-2 compared to control mice . Paired immunoglobulin-like receptor (PIR) B was previously reported to be a negative regulator of eotaxin-induced eosinophil chemotaxis and recruitment . Given this finding, Baruch-Morgenstern and colleagues sought to define the role of PIRB in EoE . Investigators observed increased Pirb expression within the esophagus of DOX-treated Cc10-rtTA;TetO-II13 mice in which surface levels of PIR-A/B were higher in esophageal eosinophils compared to other immune cell populations . Cc10-Il13 Tg ;Pirb −/− and Cc10-Il13 Tg ;Pirb +/+ mice were generated by breeding Cc10-Il13 mice with Pirb −/− mice . Significantly elevated esophageal eosinophilia and tissue remodeling occurred in DOX-treated Cc10-Il13 Tg ;Pirb −/− mice compared to Cc10-Il13 Tg ;Pirb +/+ mice. Notably, eosinophilic depletion resulted in comparable disease pathology (collagen deposition and angiogenesis) between Cc10-Il13 Tg ;Pirb −/− and Cc10-Il13 Tg ;Pirb +/+ mice . This data indicates that esophageal PIR-B possesses an inhibitory role in the development of IL-13-driven experimental EoE .

text: IL-5 is primarily produced by activated CD4 + Th cells, mast cells, and eosinophils, regulating the production, activation, and localization of eosinophils. Elevated levels of IL-5 within EoE patients correlates with increased eosinophil counts in the blood and esophagus , . IL-5 upregulates the expression of eosinophil surface receptors which enhances the migration of eosinophils from the bloodstream to esophageal tissue . Transgenic overexpression of IL-5 in mice was first explored by Dent and colleagues. The mice generated were transgenic for IL-5 overexpression under the control of the T cell promoter CD2 ( Cd2-Il5 ) . IL-5 overexpression resulted in significant increases in eosinophil accumulation in these tissues compared to wild type mice . Although this initial study did not focus on the esophagus, Mishra et al. reported that Cd2-Il5 transgenic mice display increased esophageal eosinophilia compared to wild type mice that is partially dependent on eotaxin-1 . This group later confirmed eosinophil-dependent esophageal epithelial remodeling in Cd2-Il5 transgenic mice . Another IL-5 driven model was developed by pairing esophageal IL-5 overexpression with OXA. In this model, transgenic IL-5 overexpression is under the control of the EBV-ED-L2 promoter, which is activated in esophageal epithelium. OXA was used for epicutaneous sensitization followed by intragastric challenge over a period of 12-days . At baseline, L2-Il5 mice displayed not only increased esophageal Il5 RNA expression but also robust eosinophilia within the esophagus, blood, bone marrow, and spleen. Following OXA treatment, L2-Il5 mice displayed histopathological features of EoE, including transmural infiltration of eosinophils, microabscesses, BCH, lamina propria thickening, and increased esophageal levels of IL-55, IL-13 and eotaxin-1. These phenotypes were diminished with dexamethasone . OXA-treated L2-Il5 transgenic mice also demonstrated increased levels of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Following OXA treatment, L2-Il5 mice displayed histopathological features of EoE, including transmural infiltration of eosinophils, microabscesses, BCH, lamina propria thickening, and increased esophageal levels of IL-55, IL-13 and eotaxin-1. These phenotypes were diminished with dexamethasone . OXA-treated L2-Il5 transgenic mice also demonstrated increased levels of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). Neutralizing this cytokine ameliorated EoE-associated esophageal eosinophilia, BCH and vascular remodeling, highlighting GM-CSF as a potential therapeutic target .
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Epithelial-derived IL-33 is associated with type 2 immune responses and is elevated in esophageal biopsies from EoE subjects . To explore the impact of esophageal epithelial-derived IL-33 on the innate and adaptive immune responses associated with EoE , , the EBV-ED-L2 promoter was used to drive IL-33 expression in a novel transgenic mouse. IL-33 overexpression resulted in significant esophageal tissue remodeling as evidenced by thickening of the esophageal epithelium, increased fibrosis, and subepithelial collagen deposition as well as type 2 inflammation as evidenced by eosinophil and Th2 cell infiltration concomitant with elevated levels of Il13 , Ccl11 , and Alox15 . Recently, targeting of IL-33 to the esophagus was refined by development of an inducible esophagus-targeted IL-33 transgenic mouse, allowing for temporal control of IL-33 overexpression . To generate this combined transgenic model, two initial transgenic lines were used. The first mouse (iSophagus) utilizes the ED-L2 promoter to drive the expression of rtTA in the esophageal epithelium. The second mouse (TRE33) features the tetracycline-responsible element, which drives the expression of secreted and active IL-33 in the presence of rtTA and tetracycline. Upon crossing these mice, investigators generated an inducible model of EoE (iEoE33). To induce IL-33 overexpression, mice were fed DOX-infused chow ad libitum for 2 weeks. iEoE33 mice expressed secreted IL-33 in esophageal epithelium with elevated eosinophil levels observed 5 days following DOX treatment. After 7 days of DOX exposure, BCH, DIS, and eosinophilic microabscesses were observed in esophageal epithelium. These histological changes closely resemble human EoE, validating the iEoE33 model as a relevant tool for studying EoE progression and testing potential therapeutic interventions.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: IL-18 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in host defense against infections and plays a central role in regulating the innate immune response. To enhance immune response, IL-18 induces production of IFN-γ, primarily driving Th1 responses, while also having an influence on Th2 pathways . In concert with IL-5, IL-18 aids in driving eosinophils into an activated state that promotes tissue inflammation and remodeling . Previous literature suggests a role for IL-18 in contributing to EoE inflammatory characteristics . To explore the significance of IL-18 in EoE pathology, a transgenic mouse model allowing for IL-18 overexpression was developed in which IL-18 overexpression is DOX-induced and Cc10 -driven ( rtTA-Cc10-Il18 ). Esophagi of DOX-treated rtTA-Cc10-Il18 mice displayed transmural eosinophilic and mast cell infiltration and inflammation as well as increased lamina propria thickness .
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: NF-kB-inducing kinase (NIK) is an upstream positive regulator of the noncanonical NF-kB signaling pathway, which is primarily activated by a subset of cytokines, including B-cell activating factor (BAFF). Additionally, NIK controls the maturation of immune cells, primarily B cells and dendritic cells . NIK has been reported to be dysregulated in EoE patients , . Furthermore, Clevenger, et al. showed that the expression of positive regulators of the NF-kB pathway is diminished while the expression of negative regulators of the NF-kB pathway is enhanced , indicating that suppression of NF-kB pathway may contribute to EoE pathogenesis. Given the potential influence of NIK-mediated signaling in EoE, researchers have developed genetic models to further elucidate NIK’s role in EoE pathology and identify potential novel target molecules for therapeutic interventions. Nik −/− mice were developed by Yin et al. and were reported to spontaneously develop severe eosinophilia and inflammation in various organs, including liver, lung, skin, and spleen in a T-cell-dependent manner , . Eden and colleagues then characterized the GI tract of Nik −/− mice , reporting EoE-like esophageal phenotypes, such as eosinophilia, eosinophil degranulation, mucosal thickening, BCH, and increased collagen deposition. Esophagi of Nik −/− mice also displayed increased RNA expression of Th2 ( Il4, ll13 ) and Th1 ( Il1b , Ifng , and Tnfa ) cytokines along with increased protein expression of TSLP. While more studies are needed to fully elucidate the importance of NF-kB signaling in EoE pathogenesis, currently published data demonstrates that NF-kB signaling is downregulated in EoE , . Interestingly, Eden and colleagues also reported increased expression of both NIK, and several negative regulators of NF-kB signaling within esophageal biopsies from EoE patients .
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Both environmental and genetic factors contribute to EoE disease pathogenesis . Among the variants of genes expressed by epithelial cells that are linked to EoE, approximately one-third encode proteins involved in TGF-β signaling . To understand how reduced TGF-β signaling promotes localized allergic inflammation in EoE, Laky, et al. utilized mice with the Tgfbr1 M318R variant, which eliminates TGF-β receptor (TGF-βR)1 kinase activity , knocked into the endogenous Tgfbr1 locus . These mice were bred to heterozygosity ( Tgfbr1 M318R /+ ), as homozygosity is embryonically lethal due to vascular malformations. By 6 months of age, Tgfbr1 M318R /+ mice spontaneously developed disease that clinically, immunologically, histologically, and transcriptionally recapitulated EoE. Briefly, investigators observed esophageal dilation, food impaction, eosinophilic infiltration, a lack of differentiation, hyperproliferative esophageal epithelial cells, and overexpression of innate pro-inflammatory mediators, such as Tslp and Tnfaip6 . Furthermore, investigators compared transcriptomic data of human EoE biopsies representing the 3 different EoE endotypes (EoEe1, EoEe2, and EoEe3) with their Tgfbr1 M318R /+ mice. EoEe1 encompasses those with a normal-appearing esophagus. EoEe2 biopsies exhibit an inflammatory and steroid refractory phenotype while EoEe3 exhibit a fibrostenotic phenotype with high histological severity . Their analyses revealed that the Tgfbr1 M318R /+ mice possess an esophageal transcriptional profile that correlated best with that of EoEe2 . To determine if changes within the esophagus of Tgfbr1 M318R /+ mice are epithelial cell-intrinsic, organoids derived from esophageal epithelium of Tgfbr1 M318R /+ mice were generated. These organoids displayed an EoEe2 gene signature and hyperproliferative basal cells. Additionally, lymphocyte-deficient Tgfbr1 M318R /+ mice produced an EoE phenotype that was comparable to their lymphocyte-proficient counterparts at the immunological, clinical, and histological levels.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: These organoids displayed an EoEe2 gene signature and hyperproliferative basal cells. Additionally, lymphocyte-deficient Tgfbr1 M318R /+ mice produced an EoE phenotype that was comparable to their lymphocyte-proficient counterparts at the immunological, clinical, and histological levels. Overall, this study demonstrates that TGF-βR1-mediated signaling has an epithelial-cell intrinsic role in limiting esophageal allergic inflammation and maintaining homeostasis in a lymphocyte-independent manner .

text: In addition to allergen-, chemical-, and genetic-driven models of EoE, exogenous models, in which cytokines such as IL-13, IL-18 or IL-33 are administered to the mice intranasally or via i.p. injection, have also been developed to model EoE. Intranasal or intratracheal challenge with recombinant IL-13 induces minimal dose-dependent esophageal and lung eosinophilia, and epithelial remodeling with lamina propria-infiltrating eosinophils along with BCH , , . Global STAT6, IL-5, or eotaxin-1 knockout partially ameliorated these phenotypes , . These findings further support the dependence of EoE pathogenesis on the STAT6/IL-5/eotaxin-1 signaling axis. Girkin and colleagues investigated the relationship between IL-13 and TRAIL signaling in esophageal eosinophilia by intranasally challenging mice with recombinant IL-13 . IL-13 administration led to esophageal eosinophilic infiltration as well as a STAT6-dependent increase in Trail and Mid1 expression within the esophagus. Interestingly, MID-1 silencing, but not TRAIL deficiency, led to a complete reversal of IL-13-mediated features of EoE . In addition to IL-13, increased IL-18 levels in the blood and Il-18rα RNA in the esophagus have been reported in human EoE . As such, Dutt and colleagues set out to further elucidate the role of IL-18 in EoE disease pathogenesis . Intranasal administration of recombinant IL-18 led to both mast cell and eosinophilic infiltration within the esophagus in time- and dose-dependent manners. This EoE phenotype was rescued following IL-5 or iNKT cell depletion . Although this model demonstrated the ability of IL-18 to induce EoE inflammation in mice, other histological changes were not as thoroughly explored. Il-33 expression was found to be upregulated in esophageal biopsies of active EoE patients compared to normal controls . Given this, Judd et al. sought to understand whether exogenously applied IL-33 could induce EoE symptoms within the murine esophagus.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: Il-33 expression was found to be upregulated in esophageal biopsies of active EoE patients compared to normal controls . Given this, Judd et al. sought to understand whether exogenously applied IL-33 could induce EoE symptoms within the murine esophagus. This model involves administering daily i.p. injections of recombinant human IL-33 for seven days with a final injection 1 hour prior to euthanasia. Exogenous application of IL-33 led to an EoE-like phenotype, including eosinophilic infiltration, epithelial thickening, and BCH. Moreover, increased gene signatures of eosinophils and chemotactic mediators, such as Ccl11 and Ccl12, were noted. IL-13 deficiency partially ablated the effects of IL-33 administration .
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: There are several notable differences in the murine esophagus as compared to that of the human, including the presence of a squamous forestomach and a luminal layer of keratin as well as a lack of both papillae and submucosal glands. As such, EoE has also been modeled in higher level organisms, including guinea pigs and pigs (swine). To induce experimental EoE in guinea pigs, sensitization was achieved with three i.p. injections with OVA every 48 hours. Three weeks after the last injection, guinea pigs were challenged to aerosolized OVA once a day for two weeks. These guinea pigs were shown to have esophageal eosinophilia and increased mast cell activation and degranulation – . In the swine model, young pigs were exposed to the food allergen hen egg white protein (HEWP) in which OVA is a primary component. Sensitization to HEWP was achieved via three weekly i.p. injections with oral challenge with HEWP daily for 1 week following the last sensitization. HEWP-treated pigs exhibited esophageal eosinophilia, eosinophilic abscesses, BCH, and fibrosis. In addition to histopathological changes, a Th2 immunological landscape was also observed , . The size of pigs also allows for the use of tools that are employed in clinical care of human EoE patients, including endoscopes that further permit repeated imaging and tissue collection in live animals. Despite these advantages, the use of guinea pigs and pigs can be prohibitive due to financial and space limitations associated with housing. Furthermore, mice are presently superior with regard to genetic characterization and experimental manipulation.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: As summarized above, a number of mouse models of EoE have been developed and utilized to investigate the mechanisms driving EoE pathobiology and also to test experimental therapeutics ( ; ). When utilizing in vivo models, it’s important for researchers to consider the needs of their study as well as the advantages and limitations of individual model systems. For example, while esophageal eosinophilia is a common feature of the described EoE models, remodeling in the epithelial and subepithelial compartments varies with regard to presence and extent in these models. Moreover, the localization of eosinophils varies among these models. This is true at the whole-body level with a number of models displaying eosinophilia in the esophagus as well as in circulation and other tissue sites within and beyond the GI tract, the latter of which may provide a model of eosinophilic gastrointestinal disease rather than EoE. There is also heterogeneity in terms of eosinophilia within the esophagus. A number of models report eosinophilia that is largely localized to the esophageal lamina propria while there are several model systems in which transmural eosinophilia is noted and others that feature robust epithelial eosinophilia and eosinophil-rich microabscesses. As such, the EoE phenotype that is produced should be considered when deciding how to challenge mice. Multiple models described above challenge via intragastric or intranasal delivery. Compared to intranasal challenges, intragastric administration of allergens tends to produce a more robust EoE phenotype in regard to eosinophilic infiltration, including transmural and/or intra-epithelial eosinophilia, , , , and epithelial remodeling, including BCH in the epithelium and/or fibrosis in the lamina propria , , . However, there is a risk of tearing the esophagus during gavage so care must be taken. An additional consideration is the strain of mice used.
title: Mouse Models of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Molecular and Translational Insights

text: The issue of how to differentiate EoE from GERD has confounded clinicians and researchers since the recognition of the disease. This diagnostic dilemma began with a pathology study of pediatric patients in 1982, which found that eosinophils in the esophageal squamous epithelium could be a manifestation of GERD, documented by 24-hr pH tests ( ). Pathologists rapidly accepted the concept, and it became common clinical practice to attribute esophageal eosinophilia to GERD. The first report describing EoE as a unique syndrome, characterized by solid food dysphagia and distinct from GERD by esophageal tests, was published in 1993 ( ). Subsequently, EoE was considered a chronic immune- or antigen-mediated esophageal disease. However, many cases still overlapped with GERD, so the PPI trial became the most logical and convenient means to differentiate GERD from EoE. This practice was based on the assumption that the only major effect of PPIs is to inhibit gastric acid production. Accordingly, in 2007, the American Gastroenterological Association’s consensus report defined EoE as a primary disorder characterized by esophageal symptoms, esophageal biopsies with more than 15 eosinophils per high-powered field, and the “absence” of pathologic GERD—evidenced either by normal results from pH tests or lack of response to PPIs ( ). This mutually exclusive paradigm began to fall apart as editorials raised the possibilities of a complex interaction between GERD and EoE. These raised questions such as: does EoE cause GERD? Does GERD cause EoE? Or do these merely co-exist, because GERD is such a common disease? ( ) Subsequently, Ngo et al ( ) described 3 patients with EoE and significant mucosal eosinophilia who improved, based on clinical and histological features, after 2 months of PPI therapy.
title: Presentation and Epidemiology of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

text: Does GERD cause EoE? Or do these merely co-exist, because GERD is such a common disease? ( ) Subsequently, Ngo et al ( ) described 3 patients with EoE and significant mucosal eosinophilia who improved, based on clinical and histological features, after 2 months of PPI therapy. Several years later, Molina-Infante et al ( ) published findings from 35 patients with mucosal eosinophilia (more than 15 eosinophils per high-powered field); 75% responded to rabeprazole (20 mg, twice daily) for 2 months. All 17 of the patients with GERD profile and objective acid reflux, based on endoscopy or pH tests, responded to this treatment. However, 50% of the patients with an EoE-like profile and normal pH test results also responded to the rabeprazole. The recognition of this condition, which was termed PPI-responsive esophageal eosinophilia (PPI-REE), caused further confusion. Studies documented that 23% to 61% of patients with symptomatic esophageal eosinophilia respond to PPI treatment ( ). Furthermore, the clinical, endoscopic, histologic and even esophageal gene-expression features of PPI-REE and EoE are virtually identical ( ). PPI-REE therefore resembles EoE far more than it resembles GERD. An exciting discovery around this controversy has been the recognition that EoE and GERD could each arise via cytokine-mediated esophageal injury. In contrast to the model in which refluxed acid causes a chemical injury that destroys esophageal cells, studies from patients and animal models indicated that the esophageal damage found in patients with GERD was caused by inflammatory cells, which are attracted to the esophagus by cytokines produced by esophageal epithelial cells following exposure to refluxed acid and bile ( , ). Studies of cultured esophageal epithelial cells revealed anti-cytokine effects of PPIs that were entirely independent of effects on gastric acid production—these could heal GERD and EoE.
title: Presentation and Epidemiology of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

text: Studies of cultured esophageal epithelial cells revealed anti-cytokine effects of PPIs that were entirely independent of effects on gastric acid production—these could heal GERD and EoE. Omeprazole was found to block eotaxin-3 secretion stimulated by T-helper 2 cytokines produced by esophageal cells from patients with EoE or GERD ( ) and block secretion of interleukin 8, a mediator of eosinophilic inflammation after exposure to acid and bile salts in esophageal epithelial cells from patients with GERD ( ). The current focus on how to distinguish EoE from GERD may therefore be counterproductive, since the 2 diseases often co-exist with complex interactions. Patients with GERD with the typical reflux syndrome associated with erosive esophagitis and hiatal hernia can have mucosal eosinophilia, which often is confined to the distal esophagus. It is not clear what proportion of patients with GERD present with these features, but it is likely to be less than 10% ( ). The etiology of their mucosal eosinophilia may be secondary to direct acid injury or secondary to the effects of GERD on esophageal barrier function, which renders the epithelium permeable to food antigens and causes antigen-induced esophageal eosinophilia ( ). Regardless, PPIs can reduce both mechanisms of pathogenesis; careful separation by esophageal manometry and pH – impedance testing is necessary for only patients who require surgical anti-reflux treatment.
title: Presentation and Epidemiology of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

text: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a Th2, antigen driven disease in which chronic, eosinophil rich inflammation causes symptoms of esophageal dysfunction. Esophageal symptoms due to EoE can manifest in multiple ways including heartburn/regurgitation, vomiting, dysphagia, food impactions, and even abdominal pain. The differential diagnosis for EoE is broad and can include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), parasitic and fungal infections, inflammatory bowel disease, allergic vasculitis, connective tissue disease, and other disorders associated with esophageal eosinophilia. Untreated EoE progresses to esophageal remodeling, rigidity, and luminal narrowing. – EoE diagnosis rests on the presence of esophageal eosinophilia greater than or equal to 15 eosinophils per high power field under routine light microscopy following hematoxylin and eosin staining. The diagnosis and management of EoE continues to be updated as new concepts and literature evolve. There have been 4 consensus guideline reports from the U.S. since 2006. , – The goal of this article is to provide an up to date review of the current knowledge for EoE diagnosis and its management.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Recent consensus recommendations based on a systematic review of the literature and expert opinion led to the diagnostic criteria that EoE is a clinicopathological disease characterized by (a) esophageal symptoms including but not limited to dysphagia and food impaction in adults and feeding intolerance and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) symptoms in children and (b) eosinophil predominant inflammation of ≥15 eosinophils per high power field in the esophageal tissue after exclusion of other disorders associated with similar clinical, histologic, or endoscopic features. While the initial consensus recommendations recommended a failure of twice daily or high dose proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy prior to diagnosing EoE, the latest consensus guidelines have removed this recommendation. , Although PPIs primarily provide acid blockade, they also can have anti-inflammatory effects, including decreasing IL-13 induced eotaxin-3 production. , In clinical alignment with this finding, a subgroup of patients (30–50%) who meet EoE diagnostic criteria respond clinically, histologically, and endoscopically to two months of high dose PPI therapy. – Transcription profiling using the EoE Diagnostic Panel (EDP) also shows that gene expression is identical, but less severely dysregulated, in PPI-responsive and PPI-resistant EoE. For these reasons, PPI responsive esophageal eosinophilia is now considered an EoE sub-phenotype and PPI is considered a therapeutic option for EoE.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Age-related differences in clinical presentation have been identified in children and adults. , The most common presenting symptoms in adults are dysphagia, food impaction, heartburn, and chest pain with as many as 50% of adult patients initially presenting with food impaction having a final diagnosis EoE. In contrast, children present more commonly with vomiting, heartburn, regurgitation, emesis, and abdominal pain. While younger children rarely present with dysphagia and food impaction typical of adult complaints, these presentations are commonly seen in older individuals over the age of 12 years. Several validated tools are now available to gauge symptoms in adults and children. – A multicenter study demonstrates that the pediatric symptom scoring tool PEESSv2.0 can correlate with histologic changes including eosinophilia. The Eosinophilic Esophagitis Activity Index (EEsAI) adult metric has good correlations between symptoms, histology and patient reported outcomes. Despite this, symptoms do not provide adequate EoE diagnostic or management capacity and EoE patient care requires repeated biopsy to assess for esophageal inflammation.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: The gold standard for EoE diagnosis remains the biopsy findings demonstrating increased intraepithelial esophageal eosinophils without concomitant eosinophilic infiltration in the stomach or duodenum. Since eosinophilic infiltration of the esophagus may not be evenly distributed, biopsies should be obtained from the proximal and distal esophagus to increase the diagnostic yield. At least five biopsies should be obtained at multiple esophageal levels to maximize the sensitivity based on a diagnostic threshold of ≥15 eosinophils per high power field. In addition to biopsies performed during elective endoscopy for evaluation of above symptoms, biopsies are suggested in all patients undergoing endoscopy for food impaction due to high prevalence of EoE in this subset of patients. Other histologic features of EoE include superficial layering of the eosinophils, eosinophilic micro-abscesses (clusters of ≥4 eosinophils), epithelial hyperplasia, intercellular edema or spongiosis, and eosinophil degranulation. Subepithelial fibrosis may be seen in biopsies of both children and adults with EoE. Recent investigationshave developed and validated the EoE histologic severity scoring index (HSS), a newer histologic scoring system which takes into account additional inflammatory features rather than focusing solely on the eosinophil number. The presence of eosinophilia is the key factor for a diagnosis of primary EoE so it is essential to rule out secondary causes of esophageal eosinophilia. EoE can be associated with other inflammatory intestinal diseases including inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, GERD, and extra-esophageal eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders. In some of these cases, it is important to treat the potential primary disease, for example, GERD, Crohn’s or celiac disease, appropriately and evaluate for the remission of esophageal eosinophilia. If still present, then a diagnosis of concurrent EoE and EoE-directed therapy are warranted. While eosinophils in the esophagus can be attributed to primary EoE as well as GERD, this distinction is made by clinical judgement.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: If still present, then a diagnosis of concurrent EoE and EoE-directed therapy are warranted. While eosinophils in the esophagus can be attributed to primary EoE as well as GERD, this distinction is made by clinical judgement. For instance, if a patient has erosive esophagitis, hiatal hernia, typical reflux symptoms and esophageal eosinophilia, the primary contribution in this patient is likely reflux versus EoE. In addition, it is imperative to understand EoE triggers that may be environmental or iatrogenic. A diagnosis or exacerbation of EoE during a pollen season in which a patient is exposed to a triggering antigen may resolve spontaneously. Approximately 3–5% of patients on oral immunotherapy for the treatment of food anaphylaxis are also at risk for EoE. Removal of the immunotherapeutic antigen usually results in EoE remission.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Upper endoscopy is a procedure that requires general anesthesia in children and, usually, conscious sedation in adults. As such, upper endoscopy is an invasive procedure that costs healthcare dollars as well as lost work and school time. For these reasons, research has focused on the development of less invasive tools to assess esophageal inflammation. The esophageal string test (EST) is a capsule based technology that captures eosinophil associated proteins from the esophageal lumen and has shown good correlation with eosinophilic infiltration in esophageal biopsy specimens in both children and adults. The Cytosponge is another capsule based technology originally designed for assessment of esophageal mucosa in Barrett’s esophagus and has recently been used to assess inflammation in EoE in adults. Unsedated transnasal endoscopy has been used in children and adults to assess esophageal mucosal inflammation via biopsy. , More recently, a tethered confocal microscopy capsule has been piloted in adults with EoE with preliminary data suggesting that comprehensive cellular data can be gathered for assessing of tissue inflammation. Each of these modalities show promise in being able to assess inflammation without the use of standard endoscopy. While these modalities are unlikely to replace the diagnostic or therapeutic benefits of endoscopy when a diagnosis or dilation is needed, they could have an important role in replacing repeated endoscopies for disease surveillance after treatment interventions.
section: Less invasive techniques to evaluate the esophagus
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Thickening of the deeper layers of the esophagus has been demonstrated using endoscopic ultrasound. , Mucosal and submucosal fibrosis and smooth muscle hypertrophy are likely to drive decreased esophageal compliance and to contribute to dysphagia symptoms in the absence of an identifiable stricture. , A newer technique called the endoscopic functional luminal imaging probe (endoFLIP) has demonstrated altered esophageal wall compliance in adults and children with EoE further supporting the concern for esophageal remodeling. – While esophageal diameter does not correlate with eosinophilic inflammation in adults, two pediatric studies have demonstrated that esophageal cross sectional area and compliance can align with eosinophilic inflammation, epithelial remodeling, and subepithelial fibrosis in children. , EndoFLIP can be a helpful adjunctive tool in both stricture identification and assessment when planning for esophageal dilations in adults (Gonsalves, unpublished) and esophageal rigidity can improve after treatment with either diet or medication. While histologic assessment is the gold standard in diagnosing in EoE, there have been cases in which patients with a high pretest probability of EoE have had biopsies which do not meet the diagnostic eosinophil threshold for EoE. Tissue staining for eosinophil products such as eosinophil peroxidase (EPX) may be of utility in such cases since the eosinophil “footprint” can be detected in the absence of eosinophils. While EPX staining remains a research tool, if EoE is suspected in a patient due to ancillary testing such as endoFLIP or by clinical symptoms, this can trigger a request for EPX staining by the local pathologist. The EoE diagnostic panel (EDP) is a molecular tool which may help further identify and risk stratify patients. This test assesses the expression of 96 genes that are dysregulated in EoE and has high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosis. Further, the EDP has distinguished molecular phenotypes in EoE.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: The first study to show improvement in EoE after treatment with an elemental or amino acid based diet in EoE was a case series of 10 children with suspected GERD and esophageal eosinophilia. In this landmark study, administration of an elemental diet led to symptom and inflammatory resolution in children who had failed acid blockade. Subsequently, pediatric series from several institutions confirmed an overall >90% histologic remission in EoE using amino acid formula. Two prospective adult studies of elemental diet reported a lower histologic response of approximately 75%, however both trials were limited by a 4-week treatment period and high patient nonadherence and drop out due to palatability. Overall, meta-analysis showed superiority of the elemental diet over specific food elimination diets. However, significant obstacles limit the use of amino acid formula, including taste, limited meal variety, lack of insurance coverage, and the number of endoscopies required to identify specific triggers during food reintroduction.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Initial reports began as case studies using asthma metered dose inhalers with a puff and swallow technique for esophageal deposition. Since that time, a number of formulations have been utilized in randomized, placebo controlled pediatric and adult EoE trials. – There are no FDA approved drugs for EoE in the U.S. but an orodispersable budesonide tablet is now available in Europe. , As such, patients in the U.S. are still faced with significant challenges such as proper mixing/swallowing technique and insurance coverage when using TCS for EoE. Meta-analyses of esophageal TCS in the form of fluticasone or budesonide demonstrate the superiority of TCS to placebo for esophageal eosinophilia, endoscopic findings, and symptoms. A recent meta-analysis of budesonide showed overall efficacy for all clinical endpoints with a histologic response of budesonide to placebo that demonstrated efficacy of budesonide over placebo generated an overall relative risk of 11.93 (p<0.001) in 245 pediatric and adult patients. Long term TCS therapy is indicated in EoE due to frequent recurrence with TCS removal. However, spontaneous increases in esophageal eosinophils despite continued therapy is not uncommon. , Side effects from TCS can include oral and/or esophageal candidiasis and adrenal insufficiency. However, adrenal crisis is not common and there have been no reported adverse effects on height.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Abundant data demonstrate the ability of aeroallergens to trigger and/or exacerbate EoE. , Given this, it is reasonable to test patients with EoE for aeroallergen sensitization and to educate patients about simple avoidance measures. Placebo controlled trials of subcutaneous immunotherapy for aeroallergens are not feasible for EoE but case reports document the success of aeroallergen immunotherapy for EoE and aeroallergen immunotherapy could be a reasonable adjuvant EoE therapy. There is a close link between the airway and the esophagus. Asthmatic children with EoE have higher levels of esophageal eosinophilia. Since atopic diatheses can influence one another, it is reasonable to speculate that EoE control may be improved by optimizing the management of concurrent asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eczema. To this end, it is the responsibility of the practicing allergist to treat EoE in the context of the entire allergic person.
section: Environmental allergy testing and control of concurrent atopic diatheses
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Eosinophilia is defined as an increased eosinophil count in peripheral blood, exceeding the normal range of 0.35–0.5 × 10 9 /l (3–6% of total leukocytes) [ , ▪▪ , ]. Based on absolute eosinophil count (AEC), it is classified into mild (0.5–1.49 × 10 9 /l), moderate (1.5–5.0 × 10 9 /l) and severe (>5.0 × 10 9 /l) [ ▪▪ ]. Hypereosinophilia (HE) is defined as an elevation in AEC exceeding 1.5 × 10 9 /L [ ▪▪ ]. As stated by the 2021 Working Conference on Eosinophil Disorders and Syndromes, HE is considered persistent when this threshold is recorded on two separate occasions at least two weeks apart [ ]. When HE is associated with organ damage and no alternative explanation is identified, the condition is defined as Hypereosinophilic Syndrome (HES) [ , ]. According to the ICOG-EO criteria, the diagnosis of HES requires: (i) the presence of blood and/or tissue HE, (ii) HE-associated organ damage, and (iii) exclusion of other underlying disorders or pathology as the primary cause [ , , ]. Tissue HE is defined by one or more of the following criteria: (i) eosinophils constitute more than 20% of all nucleated cells in bone marrow sections, (ii) a pathologist identifies extensive (massive) eosinophil infiltration in tissue beyond normal physiological ranges, or (iii) immunostaining reveals significant extracellular deposition of eosinophil granule proteins, such as eosinophil major basic protein (eMBP1) or eosinophil peroxidase (EPX) [ , , ]. Valent et al. highlight that tissue HE may occur without peripheral blood (PB) HE; however mild blood eosinophilia is usually observed [ ]. Originally, the definition of HES required both PB HE and HE-related organ damage, regardless of tissue HE [ , ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Valent et al. highlight that tissue HE may occur without peripheral blood (PB) HE; however mild blood eosinophilia is usually observed [ ]. Originally, the definition of HES required both PB HE and HE-related organ damage, regardless of tissue HE [ , ]. However, tissue HE with organ damage can occur without PB HE, typically involving a single organ—termed “tissue-restricted” or “organ-restricted (mono-organ) HES” [ ] (see Table for a schematic comparison of eosinophilia, HE, tissue HE, and HES, including the tissue-restricted subtype) (Fig. )
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Eosinophils are polymorphonuclear cells derived from hematopoietic precursors [ , ] and act as crucial mediators in hypereosinophilic disorders. Their development is primarily regulated by interleukin IL-3, IL-5, and granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), which promote their differentiation, survival and activation [ , , , ▪▪ ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: In response to inflammatory signals such as IL-4, IL-13, and TNF-α, various cell types produce eotaxins-particularly eotaxin-1 (CCL11) which recruit eosinophils to tissues [ , , ▪▪ ]. Upon reaching inflamed sites, eosinophils become overactivated and accumulate, initiating inflammatory responses that can lead to organ damage [ , , , ▪▪ ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Activated eosinophils release diverse mediators stored in their cytoplasmic granules, including major basic proteins (MBP1 and MBP2), eosinophil peroxidase (EPO), eosinophil cationic protein (ECP) and eosinophil-derived neurotoxin (EDN) [ , , ▪▪ ]. These granule proteins exert cytotoxic effects, contributing to tissue injury and local inflammation.
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: The combined actions of eosinophil-derived mediators result in pathological outcomes, such as leukocyte recruitment, persistent inflammation, thrombosis and fibrosis [ , , ▪▪ , ]. These processes underlie tissue damage and organ dysfunction characteristic of hypereosinophilic disorders.
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Hypereosinophilia syndrome (HES) presents a diverse array of clinical manifestations, affecting multiple organ systems with a spectrum ranging from asymptomatic to life-threatening complications. [ ▪▪ , , ] (Fig. ). The onset may be insidious, initially marked by asymptomatic eosinophilia, which can progress over years to symptomatic disease due to eosinophilic tissue infiltration and the deposition of eosinophil granules and proteins. In rarer cases, HES may have an acute onset [ , , ]
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Skin manifestations are the most common, occurring in 69% of patients [ ]. Symptoms include pruritus, urticarial lesions, and eczematous or papulonodular lesions, often seen in the lymphocytic variant of HES [ – ]. More severe presentations may include facial angioedema [ ] palpable purpura, and mucosal ulcerations [ ], especially in myeloid HES (M-HES), which may mimic Behçet's syndrome [ , , , ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Pulmonary involvement occurs in 44% of patients [ ], displaying a range of issues from rhinosinusitis and asthma to eosinophilic pneumonia. When eosinophilia extends to lung interstitium, it can lead to hypoxemia [ , , ] and eosinophilic pleural effusions, which may cause lung compression [ ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: HES is characterized by eosinophilia, often accompanied by leukocytosis and other hematologic abnormalities such as anemia and thrombocytopenia [ ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Over the years, various classifications of eosinophil disorders have been proposed [ ], typically distinguishing between primary (clonal), secondary (reactive), and idiopathic forms when the underlying causes remain elusive. In 2023, Valent categorized hypereosinophilia into four main types based on etiology and clinical characteristics [ ]: Valent also classified HES and related disorders into [ ]: Recently, the società italiana di allergologia asma e immunologia clinica (SIAAIC) task force proposed a revised classification where introduce several important conceptual distinctions [ ] (Table ). Basically in this revised classification HES subtypes include [ ]: This classification system enhances the understanding of hypereosinophilia, guiding diagnosis and potential treatment strategies [ ]. A crucial differentiation within hypereosinophilia and HES lies between the lymphocytic and myeloid variants, which refer to different pathophysiologic mechanisms, clinical presentations, and treatment approaches (Table ). The lymphocytic variant of hypereosinophilia (L-HES) is driven by clonal T-cell populations that produce cytokines (especially IL-5) to stimulate eosinophil proliferation. These T-cells are typically abnormal and the expansion of eosinophils is due to a T-cell-driven immune dysregulation rather than a primary eosinophil disorder. In conclusion, the categorization of hypereosinophilia and hypereosinophilic syndromes is still developing, and the important differences between lymphocytic and myeloid variations aid in directing diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. By comprehending these variations and how they connect to the underlying pathophysiology, clinicians may better customize interventions to meet patients’ individual needs.
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: The initial diagnostic step involves confirming the laboratory findings that demonstrate an elevated AEC. This requires two repeated blood measurements, taken at least two weeks apart, to establish persistent eosinophilia [ , ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: In the absence of reactive causes, primary clonal hypereosinophilia should be investigated through blood count, bone marrow studies, and cytogenetic/molecular testing (karyotyping, FISH, flow cytometry, RT-PCR, NGS) [ , ▪▪ , , ]. These detect key tyrosine kinase gene rearrangements -including FIP1L1::PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, and ABL1, as well as other relevant mutations [ , ▪▪ ]. RT-PCR for FIP1L1::PDGFRA is often preferred in clinical practice due to its high sensitivity [ ]. Clonality is suggested by cytopenias, thrombocytosis, polycythemia, monocytosis, basophilia and elevated vitamin B12 and tryptase levels [ , , ]. Final diagnosis should follow WHO (ICC) and ICOG-EO criteria, integrating all clinical, morphological and molecular data to guide classification and targeted therapy [ ]. Ultimately, the presence or absence of an associated HES should be addressed [ ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: In the absence of organ dysfunction, there is currently insufficient evidence to warrant initiating treatment based solely on elevated eosinophil counts. However, some specialists propose that treatment may begin at an AEC of 1.5–2 × 10 9 /l. The therapeutic approach should be tailored according to the specific etiological classification of HE or HES and the presence or absence of specific mutations.
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: The effectiveness of empirical antiparasitic therapy in unexplained chronic HE is debatable due to the lack of published evidence [ ]. There is a clinical experience with cases where empirical antiparasitic treatment permitted otherwise inexplicable HE to completely and sustainably return to normal (despite negative well conducted parasite testing). However, for a number of reasons, it might be suitable in certain situations, such the available assays and the varying sensitivity of parasite serology for stool parasite identification, in addition to the medications favorable safety and affordability. Treatment with fenbendazole or albendazole or praziquantel is indicated for any eosinophilia <1.5× 10 9 /l in the absence of an obvious cause and contraindications [ ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Given that interleukin-5 (IL-5) is a major cytokine mediating eosinophil growth and activation, several studies have assessed the potential of IL-5-targeting biologics that have been demonstrated to be a safe and efficient substitute in idiopathic HES and lymphocytic HES, the latter characterized by overproduction of IL-5 by dysregulated T cells [ , ▪▪ ] Mepolizumab has been approved for HES treatment, showing effectiveness in reducing eosinophil counts and HES flare-ups [ ]. Benralizumab 30 mg every 4 weeks showed to be noninferior to mepolizumab in adults with EGPA (but is not yet approved) [ ]. A phase II study has demonstrated the efficacy of benralizumab in PDGFRA-negative HES [ ]. A phase III, randomized, placebo-controlled study is presently being conducted to treat HES with benralizumab (clinicaltrials.gov NATRON, NCT04191304 ) . A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial is underway to evaluate the efficacy and safety of depemokimab in adults with HES ( clinicaltrials.gov DESTINY, NCT05334368 ). With its improved binding affinity for interleukin-5, depemokimab is an ultra-long-acting biologic treatment that may allow for efficient 6-month dosing intervals. Effectiveness in treating patients with severe asthma and eosinophilic phenotype has already been demonstrated [ ]. Additionally, dupilumab is a human monoclonal antibody against interleukin (IL)-4 receptor alpha that inhibits IL-4/IL-13 axis, which is responsible for several Th2-type inflammatory mechanisms including migration of eosinophils to tissues. Therefore is ongoing a study with dupilumab as add-on therapy for HES in patients with complete hematologic and partial clinical remission on eosinophil-lowering biologic agents (anti-IL-5/anti-IL5-Rα) with the aim of reduce residual pulmonary, skin, esophageal, and sinus symptoms ( clinicaltrial.gov NCT06477653 ). Table
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: Long-term monitoring of patients with HES should be individualized and based on clinical phenotype, disease severity, organ involvement, and treatment response. Regular clinical evaluations are recommended, supported by targeted instrumental assessments (such as thoracic imaging, echocardiography, and pulmonary function tests) especially for previously affected organs. Laboratory follow-up should include eosinophil counts (AEC), total immunoglobulin E (IgE), ECP, vitamin B12, serum tryptase, and inflammatory markers like CRP and ESR. This personalized approach allows for timely adjustment of therapy and detection of disease progression or relapse [ ]. Emerging biomarkers such as serum IL-5 and thymus and activation-regulated chemokine (TARC) are under evaluation for their potential role in monitoring disease activity and therapeutic response in HES [ , ]. Multidisciplinary follow-up (hematology, immunology, cardiology, dermatology) ensures comprehensive care [ , ].
title: Hypereosinophilia: clinical and therapeutic approach in 2025

text: It is debatable whether the reason for the recent high prevalence of EoE is a real increase in the incidence or increased diagnosis due to increased awareness about the disease. However, a recently published 20-year prospective, population-based study from Switzerland in the absence of EoE awareness program suggests actual increase in EoE’s incidence and prevalence ( ). In a retrospective study in all patients from a Australian provincia city with otherwise unexplained eosinophillic inflammation of the squamous epithelium, no diagnosis of EoE was made between 1981 and 1994 but 12 patients were diagnosed between 1995 and 2000 and 19 patients between 2001 and 2002 indicating a clear increase in incidence of EoE in this area. It is estimated that EoE in Westernized countries affects between 40 and 55 individuals per 100,000 population, similar to that of Crohn’s disease. Recent meta-analysis studies that surveyed the papers published in English from 1978 to 2005 show the male-to-female ratio of 3:1 with most subjects being in the 30s and 40s. , In a prospective study conducted in the United States, 31 patients with esophageal food impaction were evaluated for 3 years. Seventeen of 31 patients (54.8%) had >20 eosinophils/high-power field [HPF] without gender predilection. EoE was diagnosed in 3.4% of children with reflux symptoms and 6.8% of children with reflux esophagitis. In addition, EoE showed a higher prevalence of 68% to 94% in children with reflux symptoms not responding to proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). –
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: EoE is an immune/antigen-mediated disease in which food or environmental antigens stimulate an inflammatory response. EoE is frequently associated with allergy, although the causal relationship is not known. Rates of allergic rhinitis, asthma, and eczema in patients with EoE range from 40% to 75%, 14% to 70%, and 4% to 60%, respectively. , , The percentage of male in adults and pediatric patients is similar, 75% and 73%, respectively, while the incidence of atopic diseases including asthma, atopic dermatitis, and food allergy are more common (51% to 84%) in children than in adult patients with EoE (29% to 60%) although these diseases are prevalent in both pediatric and adult patients. In addition, seasonality associated with EoE suggests that aeroallergen may play a role in the pathogenesis of EoE. , Approximately 53% to 73% of patients with EoE are positive on the skin prick test, which is associated with exogenous allergic reactions related to serum immunoglobulin E (IgE). However, the fact that 27% to 47% of patients displayed a negative skin prick test may indicate a role of endogenous nonallergic mechanisms leading to eosinophil infiltration unrelated to IgE. Eosinophilic infiltration has been reported to be related to key cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-4, IL-5, IL-13, and eotaxin, – which stimulate the production of eotaxin-3, a potent chemokine in the esophageal mucosa. In turn, eotaxin-3 recruits and activates eosinophils to secrete proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators. IL-5 activates eosinophils, which in turn release transforming growth factor β stimulating fibroblasts and inducing fibrosis. IL-13 upregulates eotaxin-3, which recruits eosinophils in esophageal mucosa. In animal models, intratracheal administration of IL-13 induced infiltration of eosinophils in esophageal mucosa. In other words, these mediators cause eosinophilic infiltration, local tissue damage, perturb inflammatory response, and induce fibrosis, resulting in esophageal remodeling and dysfunction. ,
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: The main clinical symptoms are vomiting, dysphagia, and abdominal pain in children, whereas dysphagia with food impaction is common in adults ( ). Less common symptoms in adults are heartburn, noncardiac chest pain, odynophagia, and vomiting. , Peripheral eosinophilia appears in about 60% of pediatric patients and 5% to 50% of adult patients. Increased serum IgE, skin prick test and positive radioallergosorbent test result are observed in 40% to 73% of patients. , Normal 24-hour esophageal pH monitoring pattern is observed in more than 90% of pediatric patients and 85% to 100% of adult patients.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: EoE can be diagnosed if eosinophilic infiltration is found in esophageal epithelium. Eosinophils are not present in normal appearing mucosa, but eosinophilic infiltration can occur from various diseases, such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), eosinophilic gastroenteritis, collagen vascular disease, achalasia, and parasitic infections. , The presence of allergic history, appropriate clinical symptoms and endoscopic findings, and histopathologic findings are helpful in excluding other diseases. Few eosinophils can be observed in the mucosa (≤4 per HPF) in GERD but typical endoscopic appearance of EoE such as longitudinal furrows may not be seen in GERD. GERD is usually responsive to acid suppression but nonresponsive to steroid therapy. In 2011, diagnostic guidelines were updated. These included the followings: 1) symptoms related to esophageal dysfunction; 2) ≥15 eosinophils per HPF in at least one esophageal biopsy specimen, with few exceptions; 3) eosinophilia limited to the esophagus; and 4) other causes of esophageal eosinophilia excluded, particularly PPI-responsive esophageal eosinophilia (PPI-REE) ( ). Several studies have shown that more than one-third of patients with esophageal eosinophilia respond to PPI treatment. However, it is unknown whether PPI-REE is a separate, new disease entity, an atypical manifestation of GERD, or a variant form of EoE that responds to PPI. In 2012, Dellon suggested a novel diagnostic algorithm for EoE ( ), in which EoE must be suspected clinically at first followed by endoscopy with biopsy. To differentiate the other causes of esophageal eosinophilia, in particular GERD or PPI-REE, endoscopy with biopsy is recommended after a trial of PPI for 8 weeks.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: A number of studies have reported several typical endoscopic features of EoE: fixed esophageal rings (corrugated rings or trachealinization), transient esophageal rings (felinization), whitish exudate or papules, longitudinal furrows, small/narrow-caliber esophagus, and mucosal laceration induced by passage of endoscope (fragile crêpe paper-like appearance). , We previously studied the concordance rate and clinical predictors of EoE in endoscopically suspected eosinophilic esophagitis (EsEoE). Of 17 patients with EsEoE, five were finally confirmed as EoE by histology (diagnostic concordance rate, 29.4%). In a study by Sgouros et al . , normal endoscopic finding was observed in only 8.8% of the patients with EoE. The most common endoscopic findings of EoE are mucosal or linear sheering after the passage of the endoscope (59.3%), rings or corrugated esophagus (49.2%), strictures (39.7%), whitish exudates or papules (15.7%), and narrow/small-caliber esophagus (5.3%). Additionally, longitudinal furrows, diminished/lost vascularity, and fragile crêpe paper-like appearance are observed. Longitudinal furrow, as shown in , was the most common endoscopic finding (6/9, 66.7%), and only one of nine patients with EoE presented normal looking mucosa (11.1%). We concluded that patients with dysphagia with two or more of the aforementioned endoscopic findings were more suggestive of EoE. However, we did not find positive correlation between eosinophil density in biopsy specimens, clinical symptoms, and endoscopic features. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) reveals that longitudinal furrows present as topographical changes caused by thickening of mucosa and submucosa. Thickened esophageal wall combined with mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria was found in EoE using EUS. Therefore, causes of dysphagia and/or food impaction may be explained by thickened muscle layer consisting of muscular dysfunction.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: EoE is characterized by a dense eosinophilic infiltrate into the epithelium of the squamous esophagus, as shown in . To optimize pathologic diagnosis, endoscopic biopsy should be taken from the proximal and distal esophagus, since eosinophils are not evenly distributed within the esophageal mucosa. Eosinophilic infiltration should be absent in gastric and duodenal mucosa. The optimal number of biopsies is essential for accurate diagnosis. The diagnostic sensitivity of 2, 3, and 6 biopsy specimens are 84%, 97%, and 100%, respectively. EoE is also characterized by the formation of microabscesses by eosinophil infiltration in the superficial layer of the esophageal epithelium, which is observed in 25% to 45% of the patients with EoE. , The histologic picture of eosinophilic microabscess is shown in . It is not observed in patients with GERD or peptic esophagitis. Infiltration of the superficial layer by eosinophils lasts after acid blockade therapy for at least 2 months. Noncharacteristic findings, such as basal zone hyperplasia and increased papillary size are also observed. In our previous study, associated features included degranulation (100%), spongiosis (91.7%), and eosinophilic microabscess (58.3%). The 2011 diagnostic guideline describes more than 15 eosinophils/HPF in at least one esophageal biopsy specimen, with few exceptions, and eosinophilia limited to the esophagus. “Few exception” are defined as those patient with <15 eosinophils/HPF with other features of eosinophilic inflammation including microabscess formation, superficial layering or extracellular eosinophil granules.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Peripheral eosinophilia is found in 40% to 50% of patients with EoE, and its count decreases after successful treatment with topical corticosteroids. , Peripheral eosinophilia is correlated with the number of esophageal eosinophils. Serum total IgE levels are increased in 50% to 60% of patients with EoE, , although its level does not reflect either histologic inflammation or predictor of therapeutic response. The skin prick test (SPT) is an immediate type allergic test for food allergen and aeroallergen. , SPT is warranted in detecting food allergy associated with EoE, although the usefulness of therapeutic application including specific food avoidance by its positivity is still limited and requires more study to validate its significance.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: It is helpful to identify the algorithmic process for diagnosis and proper treatment, prior to undertaking major treatment including corticosteroids. The goal of the treatment would be complete symptom relief and resolution of esophageal eosinophilia. To exclude other causes of esophageal eosinophilia such as GERD and PPI-REE, an 8-week trial of high-dose PPI and repeat endoscopy are recommended. PPIs have anti-inflammatory effects by reducing eosinophils by decreasing Th2 cytokine-stimulated eotaxin-3 mRNA expression and protein secretion independent of the effects on acid production. , In fact, several studies have reported that one-third or more patients with esophageal eosinophilia responded to PPI treatment. Therefore, it has been suggested that PPIs might not distinguish EoE from GERD. If EoE is confirmed, diet therapy and topical corticosteroid to suppress immune response will be initiated. When evidence of fibrostenotic disease, such as narrow-caliber esophagus or stricture, is present, endoscopic dilation is effective in improving the symptoms. After the treatment, symptoms and eosinophil counts are generally improved, but endoscopic findings may not be improved, indicating that deformity of esophageal structure, or remodeling due to eosinophilic inflammation is irreversible.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: The use of steroids is one of the mainstays of pharmacologic treatment. Oral corticosteroid therapy improves the symptoms within 1 week when administered for 1 month, but systemic steroids use is associated with side effects. Whereas topical steroids, such as flucatisone and budesonide, known as swallowed inhaled steroid therapy, are effective treatments for improvement of symptoms and resolution of esophageal eosinophilia. In a study in adults that included 21 patients who were administered topical steroids for 6 weeks, all patients had relief of dysphagia that lasted a minimum of months. Dry mouth was the only adverse effect noted and esophageal candidiasis was not reported. Three patients relapsed after 4 months. Recommended doses of corticosteroid treatment protocol for EoE are shown in . If topical steroids are stopped after initial treatment, most of them recurred. But, there is little data regarding the effectiveness of maintenance treatment. Long-term maintenance treatment with low dose budesonide (0.5 mg/day) for 50 weeks was more effective than placebo in maintaining EoE in clinical and histologic remission, although the optimal duration and dose of budesonide are not yet clarified.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: Immunotherapy related to allergic medications includes the leukotriene D4 receptor antagonist and anti-IL-5. Montelukast, a selective inhibitor of the leukotriene D4 receptor, is also used for the treatment of asthma in adults. In a study reported by Attwood et al . , eight adult patients with EoE was started on 10 mg per day dose of montelukast but the dose was increased up to 100 mg daily if required. Once symptom was relieved, the dose was reduced to maintenance levels between 20 and 40 mg per day. Six of eight patients reported complete subjective improvement and five patients remained completely asymptomatic. However, the safety of the high dose used in this study is unclear. Montelukast could not completely treat the infiltration of eosinophils in the esophageal tissue. Cromolyn sodium, a mast cell stabilizer, is not thought to have apparent therapeutic benefit in patients with EoE. A study conducted with mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against IL-5, suggested improvement in patient with EoE in clinical symptoms, endoscopic findings, and histologic findings. However, the long-term effect or safety of this drug need to be further investigated. Additionally, anti-IL-13 monoclonal antibodies, antieotaxin-3, anti-IgE antibodies and anti-inflammatory drugs have been used either to treat EoE or under development. , However, these biologic agents are not yet in clinical practice in patients and require further scientific evidence.
section: 3. Leukotriene antagonist, mast cell stabilizer, and other biologic drugs
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: EoE is a chronic, immune/antigen-mediated esophageal disease characterized by eosinophilic infiltration and typical clinical presentation includes dysphagia and food impaction due to fibrostenosis associated with inflammatory changes and alteration of biomechanical properties. Endoscopic examination reveals mucosal fragility, longitudinal furrows, ring or corrugated mucosa, whitish papules, or small caliber esophagus. After exclusion of other causes of esophageal eosinophilia including PPI-REE or GERD, the tailored treatment of diet therapy, corticosteroids, and/or endoscopic dilation is considered according to its phenotype of whether inflammatory and/or fibrostenotic changes in the esophagus. Further basic and clinical research data are needed to understand its pathophysiology, biomarkers, clinical courses and to update the diagnostic algorithm and develop novel treatments.
title: An Overview of Eosinophilic Esophagitis

text: The first descriptions in the scientific literature of infection by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus‐2 (SARS‐CoV‐2), referred to as coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19), date back to early 2020. Within a few weeks, the first reports of haematological abnormalities were published in different phases of the disease. These first observations were confirmed by studies of numerous patients with COVID‐19. , , At this point, 2.5 years after the start of the pandemic, there is now in‐depth knowledge of the haematological alterations characteristic of the infection, of their frequency in disease of different severity and requiring a different level of care (intensive care vs. non‐intensive care), and of the evolution in the different phases of the disease, up to recovery or death, , including long‐term alterations in recovered patients. Some clinical correlations and their potential value as a more or less unfavourable prognostic indicator of evolution are well established for some anomalies. , Quantitative abnormalities of haematological variables measured in the full blood count (FBC) have been described in early works on large COVID‐19 patient groups and have recently been updated with new controlled studies , , and reviews. , , In most cases, anaemia is absent, mild or moderate, and, in pathogenetic terms, of the hyporegenerative form usually associated with inflammatory and infectious diseases. Anaemia can be more severe in COVID‐19 cases with microangiopathic and haemorrhagic complications from disseminated intravascular coagulation. In these same patients, platelet counts, which are otherwise often normal, can also decrease markedly. The occasional anaemia and thrombocytopenia can have prognostic implications. The more consistent abnormality of white blood cells (WBCs) is lymphocytopenia, which is frequent in all hospitalised patients and, differing from CD4 + lymphocytopenia of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, does not involve a specific subpopulation but rather all lymphocyte subsets to an often indistinguishable extent.
title: Coronavirus disease 2019 ( COVID ‐19): Focus on peripheral blood cell morphology
